title: Bootstrap
dek: Replace the unknown sampling distribution of T(Y) with the distribution of T(Y*) under resampling from a fitted world — empirical or parametric.
story: The bootstrap is not “sampling with replacement because computers are cheap.” It is a plug-in estimate of a sampling distribution: the world F is unknown, so use F̂, draw Y* ~ F̂, and look at T(Y*) − T(Y) as a stand-in for T(Y) − θ.

Nonparametric bootstrap resamples rows of the observed sample (or clusters, if you have clusters). Parametric bootstrap resamples from f(· | θ̂). They coincide in large n for well-specified regular models and diverge when the model is wrong or the statistic is not a smooth function of F.

Percentile intervals, basic (pivotal) intervals, and BCa intervals are different mappings from the bootstrap sample of T* to a set. A histogram of T* is not yet an interval, and it is not a posterior.
deepTitle: When the resample is the right experiment
deep: IID rows: resample isolates. Clustered surveys: resample districts, keeping isolates inside a district together. Phylogenies: a naive site bootstrap is a different scientific claim (uncertainty in the alignment given a tree model) than resampling independent lineages.

Failure modes: n too small, T not Hadamard-differentiable (sample quantiles at 0, MLE on a boundary, max statistic), and dependence you did not resample. If 30% of bootstrap MLEs hit π* = 0, the percentile interval is a portrait of the boundary, not a 95% coverage machine.

Parametric bootstrap of an LRT: simulate from the fitted null, recompute Λ*, and use the simulated tail instead of χ². This is often the right reference when regularity is doubtful and n is modest — more honest than a starred p from software defaults.
Bayesian posterior sampling is not a bootstrap. You can compare a posterior interval to a bootstrap interval as a robustness check; you may not caption a bootstrap histogram as p(θ | y).

formulas.label: Bootstrap plug-in
formulas.expression: L(F̂)  ≈  law of T(Y*) − T(Y)  as a stand-in for  law of T(Y) − θ
formulas.note: Y* ~ F̂. Choose F̂ empirical or parametric.

formulas.label: Percentile interval
formulas.note: Simple, not always best calibrated. Basic interval uses 2T − T*.

visual.caption: Bootstrap as a loop: fit F̂ from the observed sample, resample, recompute T, collect the cloud of T*. The cloud estimates a sampling law, not a posterior of θ.

example.title: Cluster bootstrap for a district survey
example.setup: 12 districts, unequal nⱼ, estimator: survey mean of a binary FQ-R call with no hierarchical model, just a weighted mean π̂. Naive iid row bootstrap would pretend isolates are the independent units.

steps.title: Wrong resample
steps.body: Drawing isolates with replacement ignores the district cluster. The bootstrap SE will be too small if within-district correlation is positive — the usual TB-survey fact.

steps.title: Right resample
steps.body: Draw 12 districts with replacement, keep each district’s isolates intact, recompute the weighted mean. That estimates the sampling law of the survey design you actually ran (approximately).

steps.title: What the cloud will show
steps.body: With 12 clusters the T* histogram will be lumpy. That lumpiness is information: n_cluster = 12 is the effective experiment. A smooth Normal SE from 400 isolates was the fiction.

example.takeaway: Resample the independent pieces of the design. Sites, reads, and SNPs are usually not those pieces.

check.prompt: A nonparametric bootstrap histogram of T* estimates:
choices: The posterior of θ under a flat prior
The sampling distribution of T under a plug-in world F̂
The bias of every competing estimator
check.answer: The sampling distribution of T under a plug-in world F̂
check.why: That is the plug-in principle. It is not Bayes unless you add a prior and a different algorithm.

whyWrong.The likelihood function L(θ | y): L is a curve in θ, not a histogram of T*.
whyWrong.The bias of every competing estimator: You can estimate bias of this T; not magic for all T.

check.prompt: B = 1000 bootstrap copies of a mean, sd(T*) = 0.04. A bootstrap SE for the mean is:
check.why: The bootstrap SE is the SD of the T* cloud, already on the scale of T, not divided by √B. B is Monte Carlo precision of that SD.

whyWrong.0.04/√1000: That would be an SE of a Monte Carlo mean of T*, not the SE of T.
whyWrong.1.96×0.04: That is a half-width, not the SE.

check.prompt: On the bootstrap flow plate, the loop labelled “B times” is there because:
check.figureHint: Arrow from draw y* back toward F̂.
choices: One resample already is the sampling distribution
Monte Carlo approximation of the plug-in law needs many T(y*)
B is the sample size n
check.answer: Monte Carlo approximation of the plug-in law needs many T(y*)
check.why: The bootstrap distribution is a probability law; B draws approximate it.

whyWrong.B is the sample size n: B is the number of resamples.
